newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Sun rises over colonial Hong Kong for last time.
newsitem.headline: Sun rises over colonial Hong Kong for last time.

text.p: The sun rose over colonial Hong Kong for the last time on Monday as a billion mainland Chinese readied to embrace it after 156 years of British rule.
First light found a city in repose. Victoria Peak, the island's main landmark, was draped in mist and the city's soaring office towers were silent.
Even Hong Kong harbour, usually churning with ferries, was oddly quiet before the historic day's traffic began.
Joggers wound through city streets where a few couples embraced in the shadows and party-goers straggled home.

Christian Schonfeldt, a Danish businessman who grew up and lives in Hong Kong, was in the streets of the entertainment district Wan Chai at dawn in a tuxedo, having spent the night celebrating his brother's wedding.
"It's true I've had a few beverages but it has been a great night and it's a wonderful time to be in Hong Kong," the 27-year old said.
"The handover won't slow Hong Kong down. The biggest investors here are mainland Chinese themselves. Things may be unsettled for a few months but the future is still here and in Shanghai."
A British military guard raised the Union Jack over a monument to the dead of two World Wars at a solemn 7:00 a.m. ceremony attended by several hundred residents and tourists.
Sweat soaked through the khaki tunics of three Black Watch soldiers who raised the flag.
The ceremony was the official start of an exhausting day of pomp and pageantry culiminating in the transfer, at midnight, of Hong Kong from Britain to China.
"The handover is orderly but the Chinese are behaving as though they won't be around on July 1," said Peter Hale, a 39-year old British businessman at the flag raising.

"Yesterday the Chinese were taking pictures of everything as though it were about to disappear. For the Westerners here the handover is a big party. Who knows what's on the minds of the Chinese? For them the future is a bit of a question mark."
Half a million people are expected to line the waterfront to watch an evening fireworks spectacular and 100 million viewers around the world could see the handover on television.
The harbour-front venues for the main handover ceremonies were virtually deserted on Monday, sealed off by police.
Where thousands of tourists and residents swarmed on Sunday, taking souvenir snapshots of themselves with departing British servicemen, only police and an occasional journalist roamed.
The royal yacht Britannia on which Britain's Prince Charles and Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten steam out of the territory shortly after midnight, shifted gently at its mooring.
Royal Marines toting automatic weapons, stood watch over the British frigate HMS Chatham alongside Britannia.
Across the street, a soldier from the Black Watch regiment in their distinctive green and black kilt guarded the gate to the Prince of Wales barracks.
On Tuesday, a soldier of China's People's Liberation Army takes his place.
A Chinese man at the Star Ferry terminal summed up his feelings about Hong Kong's last day under British rule.
"Hong Kong has always been Chinese, never British. The British came and now they are going," the man said. "What's 150 years in the history of a country as old as China? It's nothing."
